abstract.t: RFC 8693 defines the act claim for multi-hop actor identification in JWTs but does not record per-hop authorization constraints or provide delegator cryptographic confirmation. This specification defines the delegation_chain JWT claim as a structured companion to act: an ordered array of delegation records capturing the authorization constraints delegated at each hop (expressed as scope, with an opaque reference for deployments that use structured authorization constraints), each record carrying the delegating agent's cryptographic confirmation. The companion root_authorization_ref claim references the original user authorization from which the chain derives. act and delegation_chain together provide runtime authorization and verifiable delegation lineage. The specification defines the validation rules a Resource Server applies to the chain, the Token Exchange flow through which chains are extended, and how a chain crosses trust domain boundaries with the JWT authorization grant of OAuth identity chaining, in which each record additionally carries the attestation of the Authorization Server that created it.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: In multi-agent systems, a primary agent (Agent A) may need to delegate a subset of its authorized operations to a secondary agent (Agent B), which may in turn delegate further to Agent C. Each delegation hop must preserve the original user's authorization intent while constraining what each downstream agent is permitted to do.

OAuth 2.0 already provides building blocks for expressing delegation. RFC 8693 defines the act claim, which supports nested multi-hop actor identification (enabling a token to express that Agent A delegated to Agent B, which in turn delegated to Agent C). defines the cross-domain transport pattern combining Token Exchange () and JWT Authorization Grant () to carry identity and authorization information across trust domain boundaries. These mechanisms address the runtime side of delegation: who is currently acting, and how to move tokens across domains.
However, two structural gaps remain for agent delegation scenarios:

ul.li: Per-hop authorization constraints: The act claim identifies the actors at each hop but does not record what authorization constraints were applied at each delegation step. A downstream Resource Server sees the final scope but cannot verify whether intermediate agents narrowed or expanded the authorization along the way.

Delegator cryptographic confirmation: The act claim is constructed unilaterally by the Authorization Server. The delegating agent leaves no independent cryptographic evidence that it authorized a specific delegation. This limits non-repudiation and post-hoc audit capabilities.

section.t: This specification introduces the delegation_chain claim as a structured companion to act. While act provides runtime actor identification for authorization decisions, delegation_chain records the full delegation history as an ordered array of delegation records. Each record captures the authorization constraints delegated at that hop and carries the delegator's cryptographic confirmation, so that neither the Authorization Server nor any delegating agent can unilaterally construct or deny a delegation record. The token also carries a root_authorization_ref claim referencing the original user authorization from which the chain derives, so that downstream verifiers can check that no hop exceeds it. The claims coexist in the same token: act identifies the current actor for the Resource Server, and delegation_chain records how the authorization was delegated, step by step, for verification and compliance systems.

The delegation_chain claim addresses delegation lineage and verification, complementing the runtime semantics provided by existing OAuth mechanisms. Cross-domain delegation () addresses the multi-domain scenario. This version of the specification focuses on linear delegation chains; other complex topologies such as diamond-shaped delegation, where multiple paths converge on the same agent, may be addressed by future extensions.

Scope Boundary: This specification addresses problems that lie outside the design scope of Token Exchange () and Identity Chaining (). Token Exchange defines how to convert one token into another but does not record the delegation lineage across multiple hops. Identity Chaining defines how to transport identity across trust domains but intentionally leaves Claims Transcription representation undefined. The two problems addressed by this specification, multi-hop delegation lineage and delegator non-repudiation, are separate from both token conversion and cross-domain transport. Merging this mechanism into either existing specification would broaden its scope beyond its original design intent and impose delegation lineage complexity on deployments that do not need it.

This specification defines the delegation lineage mechanism. The structure of delegated authorization constraints, when carried by reference, is deployment-specific and out of scope of this specification; the consent lifecycle and evidence model belong to separate work.

Relationship to Compositional Approaches: composes existing OAuth mechanisms (Token Exchange, Transaction Tokens, and CIBA) to address agent authentication and authorization. Composition of existing mechanisms alone does not provide per-hop delegator cryptographic confirmation or a verifiable delegation history; that is the layer this specification defines. The two approaches can be used together: compositional frameworks provide the transport and runtime semantics, and delegation_chain provides the structured delegation record and non-repudiation layer.

Relationship to Cross-App Access (ID-JAG): The Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) () profiles Identity Chaining for Cross-App Access (XAA): an application obtains an access token for a third-party API by presenting an identity assertion brokered through the IdP that the downstream Resource Authorization Server already trusts for single sign-on and subject resolution. ID-JAG addresses the identity side of that exchange; its AI agent use case covers a single agent acting as an OAuth client of external tools on behalf of a user. The specification itself marks what it leaves open on the delegation side: it "does not define normative processing requirements for actor_token or whether an act claim is included in the issued ID-JAG", and, beyond requiring that the same ID-JAG not be reused for a different downstream Resource Authorization Server, it leaves propagation across additional downstream hops to "other mechanisms" that "MAY be used", without defining how authorization propagates and narrows along the way.

This specification defines such a mechanism, and the mapping to the gaps above is direct. For the actor delegation that ID-JAG defers to future extensions, this specification defines the delegation record, the delegator's per-hop cryptographic confirmation, and the rules for constructing act when delegation_chain is present (). For the downstream-hop gap, the delegation_chain claim carries the per-hop scope and constraint lineage that a downstream Resource Server verifies (), independently of the IdPs that resolved the subjects at each boundary. For the single-agent use case, the wit:// and spiffe:// agent identifiers () extend the model to agent-to-agent delegation. The two specifications compose at the root authorization: an AS MAY verify the user's identity for the first delegation using an identity assertion grant (), after which delegation_chain records how authorization flowed from that root to the token presenter. ID-JAG resolves who the subject is at a trust boundary; delegation_chain records how the authorization was delegated from that subject.

section.title: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

section.title: Relationship to Existing Mechanisms
section.t: This section describes how the delegation_chain claim relates to existing OAuth 2.0 mechanisms, establishing the precise boundary between runtime delegation semantics and structured delegation records.

section.title: Relationship to the act Claim
section.t: RFC 8693 defines the act claim to express that delegation has occurred and to identify the acting party. The act claim supports nested multi-hop actor chains: a token can express that Agent A delegated to Agent B, which delegated to Agent C, all within a single nested JSON structure. This nesting enables Resource Servers to identify the current actor and trace the actor lineage for authorization decisions.

The act claim is constructed by the Authorization Server alone: the AS assembles the nested actor chain without requiring independent proof from each delegating agent. This is sufficient for runtime authorization decisions but does not capture per-hop policy constraints or delegator consent.

These properties cannot be added to act itself. The act claim carries no authorization content: it records who acted on whose behalf, but not what authorization was granted at each hop. Its processing model, as defined by , is an AS-attested identity statement: an implementation that understands act validates the actor chain as issued by the Authorization Server and would ignore additional members carrying per-hop signatures or constraints, silently accepting a token whose delegation evidence it did not check. Defining per-hop evidence inside act would therefore change the meaning of an existing, deployed claim, which is a matter for the base specification rather than for an extension. The delegation lineage is consequently defined as a separate claim, and act retains its RFC 8693 semantics unchanged.

The delegation_chain claim complements act by recording the delegation lineage as a structured array of records. Each record captures the authorization constraints applied at that hop (scope, and, when present, policy_ref) and the delegator's own cryptographic proof (delegator_signature), which is REQUIRED on every record. Records created by an Authorization Server other than the issuer of the token carrying the chain additionally carry that AS's attestation (as_signature). This enables:

ul.li: Per-hop policy constraints: Each delegation record carries the authorization applied at that hop, not just the final scope. This preserves the full delegation lineage and enables scope narrowing verification.
Delegator proof: The delegator_signature on each record provides independent evidence of each delegator's consent, enabling non-repudiation that the AS alone cannot provide.
Root authorization reference: The root_authorization_ref claim references the original user authorization, enabling downstream verifiers to check that no hop exceeds it.

section.t: A token that carries delegation_chain MAY also carry a flat act claim for compatibility with Resource Servers that implement . In a token carrying both claims, act identifies the current actor for the Resource Server's authorization decision, while delegation_chain provides the structured delegation record from the current actor back to the original human principal. The delegatee_id of the most recent delegation record (index 0) MUST match the act.sub value, ensuring continuity between the two claims. The current delegatee is identified by delegation_chain record 0 whether or not act is present.

, Section 4.4, expresses multi-hop delegation by nesting act claims within one another, the least recent actor being the most deeply nested. This specification defines a different representation for tokens carrying the delegation_chain claim: in such tokens the act claim contains a single sub value (the current delegatee) and MUST NOT contain a nested act claim. The actor lineage is conveyed by the delegation_chain array instead of nested act claims, so that it is independently verifiable and carries per-hop constraints. Authorization Servers MUST NOT nest act claims in tokens that carry delegation_chain, and Resource Servers MUST NOT expect nested act claims in such tokens. delegation_chain is thus a companion claim that reuses act for current-actor identification while taking over the multi-hop lineage role of nested act claims with a separately verifiable structure.

, Section 4.1, defines the may_act claim, which states that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party. may_act and delegation_chain are complementary: an Authorization Server MAY use may_act in an issued token to pre-authorize specific delegatees for a subsequent delegation hop, in which case a delegation request naming a delegatee matching may_act is a candidate for authorization without further permission checks. The delegation_chain record then captures the hop that may_act enabled. Whether a given delegation is permitted is determined by AS policy, expressed through may_act, a delegation scope, or other deployment-specific means; this specification defines how a permitted delegation is represented and validated.

section.title: Relationship to Identity Chaining
section.t: defines a general-purpose pattern for preserving identity and authorization information across trust domains, combining Token Exchange () and JWT Authorization Grant (). It addresses the transport side of cross-domain delegation: how to move a token from Domain A to Domain B while preserving the user identity and authorization context.
This specification reuses the identity chaining transport for cross-domain delegation () and adds agent-specific extensions:

ul.li: Constraint narrowing enforcement: Each delegation hop carries a scope equal to or narrower than its predecessor; structured constraints (policy_ref) are attested by the issuing AS when present;
Per-hop signatures: The delegating agent signs each delegation record, and records that cross a domain boundary additionally carry the creating AS's attestation, preventing unilateral forgery;
Agent Identifier URIs: Resolvable URI-based identity for delegators and delegatees, supporting WIT and SPIFFE schemes.

section.t: The two differ in deployment scope: identity chaining addresses general cross-domain identity propagation (human users, CI/CD pipelines, SSO extension), while this specification profiles that transport specifically for agent-to-agent delegation with delegation lineage requirements.

section.title: Relationship to Claims Transcription
section.t: Section 2.5 of defines Claims Transcription (the process by which Authorization Servers add, change, or remove claims when producing JWT authorization grants or access tokens during cross-domain flows). That specification explicitly leaves the representation of transcribed claims undefined: "The representation of transcribed claims and their format is not defined in this specification."

The delegation_chain claim provides one such representation. When delegation crosses a trust domain boundary, each delegation record captures the transcribed authorization constraints (scope, and when present policy_ref) and the cryptographic evidence of the transcribing parties (the delegator via delegator_signature, and the AS that created the record via as_signature). This enables the receiving domain to verify what was transcribed, who authorized the transcription, and under what constraints, which addresses the representation gap left by identity chaining.

Implementations using identity chaining for cross-domain delegation SHOULD include the delegation_chain claim in the JWT authorization grant as a structured Claims Transcription format, enabling the receiving AS to validate the delegation lineage before issuing a local access token.

section.title: Relationship to Refresh Tokens and Async Refresh
section.t: This specification builds on refresh tokens (); it does not replace them. A refresh token expresses a 1:1 relationship between a client and an Authorization Server: when it is used, the AS re-evaluates and issues a new access token, but the refresh exchange itself carries no record of who authorized what, at which hop, under which constraints. A delegation_chain records exactly that: an N-hop lineage in which each hop carries its own authorization constraints, signatures, and evidence anchor, with scope narrowing propagated along the chain. The two compose: refresh tokens remain the mechanism through which a client obtains fresh access tokens, and the delegation_chain in the issued token preserves the delegation lineage across those refreshes. Concretely, when an Authorization Server issues a new access token in a refresh exchange for a delegated token, it MUST carry the delegation_chain of the refreshed token unchanged: a refresh is not a delegation event and MUST NOT prepend, modify, or drop records.

The asynchronous refresh problem for delegation chains, in which a chained token expires while the user is offline and an agent must refresh it without widening privileges, breaking the identity chain, or impersonating the user, is addressed by Delegated Refresh Tokens for OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (). That specification defines the refresh of delegation chains; this specification defines the chain structure that is being refreshed. The two are complementary and can be combined.

dl.dd: An agent that transfers a subset of its authorization to another agent.
An agent that receives delegated authorization from a delegator.
A single transfer of authorization from one agent to another.
An ordered sequence of delegation hops from the most recent back to the original authorization.
The original authorization granted by a human principal, from which all delegations derive.

A token that cryptographically attests to the identity of a workload or agent, typically issued by a workload identity provider. A WIT URI is a URI that identifies a specific agent and references the WIT bound to that agent's identity.

A URI used to identify a delegating or delegatee agent in a delegation record. This specification defines two URI schemes for agent identifiers: WIT URIs (wit://) and SPIFFE IDs (spiffe://). The identifier MUST be resolvable to a verifiable public key for signature verification.

section.t: The delegation_chain is an ordered array of delegation records, from most recent to earliest. Each record represents one delegation hop. A token carrying a delegation_chain claim also carries the root_authorization_ref claim ().

section.title: The root_authorization_ref Claim
section.t: The root_authorization_ref claim is an opaque identifier referencing the root authorization event: the original authorization granted by the human principal from which all delegations in the chain derive. It MUST be present in every access token that carries a delegation_chain claim. The chain records how authorization was delegated between agents; the root authorization itself is not recorded as a chain entry, because the delegator of every chain record is an agent with a resolvable key, whereas the root authorization originates from the human principal through the initial OAuth flow. The root_authorization_ref claim is the pointer that anchors the chain to that origin.

The format of the identifier and the mechanism for resolving it are deployment-specific: deployments using a structured authorization evidence model SHOULD set this value to the identifier of the root token's evidence claim; other deployments MAY use any stable, unique identifier (e.g., a consent record ID or an audit log entry reference) that enables post-hoc retrieval of the original authorization context. This specification treats the value as opaque. When the AS issues a delegated token, it propagates the root_authorization_ref claim from the subject token, and the receiving AS of a cross-domain flow propagates it from the JWT authorization grant, so that every token in the lineage anchors to the same root authorization.

section.title: Delegation Lifecycle
section.t: A delegation record transitions through three phases during its lifecycle:

ol.li: Delegation Proposal Phase: The delegating agent creates a delegation proposal that includes the delegatee identity, the delegated scope, and, when structured constraints are used, a reference to them, and signs the prospective record with the key that its delegator_id resolves to.

Delegation Enforcement Phase: The Authorization Server validates the delegation request, verifies the delegator's token, verifies the delegator's signature on the delegation_proposal, and issues the delegation record upon successful validation. For the first delegation (User to Agent A), the AS MAY additionally verify the user's identity using an identity assertion grant ().
Chain Propagation Phase: The delegation record is embedded into an access token's delegation_chain claim, enabling multi-hop propagation within or across trust domains.

section.t: This three-phase model cryptographically binds the root authorization reference, agent identities, and policy constraints at every hop. Whether the Authorization Server requires user consent before authorizing a delegation hop is AS policy and is out of scope of this specification; the mechanism for obtaining such consent, when required, is likewise out of scope.

section.title: Field Definitions

tr.td: A URI identifying the delegating agent. This specification defines two URI schemes: wit:// (WIT URI) and spiffe:// (SPIFFE ID). The URI MUST be resolvable to a verifiable public key for delegator_signature verification.
A URI identifying the receiving agent. The same URI scheme considerations as delegator_id apply.

The delegated scope at this hop, expressed as a space-delimited list of scope values (, Section 3.3). REQUIRED when the chain contains more than one record, so that scope narrowing along the chain is verifiable by any holder of the token; MAY be omitted on single-record chains, where the delegated scope is conveyed by the access token's scope claim. When present, this field captures the scope explicitly authorized at this hop and is included in the signature computation to prevent scope expansion by a compromised AS. The Resource Server verifies that scope narrows monotonically along the chain ().

An opaque reference to the structured authorization constraints that apply to this delegation hop, for deployments that use a structured constraint model. The format and resolution mechanism of the reference are deployment-specific; this specification treats the value as opaque (the same treatment as root_authorization_ref). The referenced constraints MUST NOT expand the delegator's authorization; this is enforced by the Authorization Server at issuance time and attested by the record's signatures. When absent, the delegated constraints are expressed solely by scope.

Cryptographic signature from the delegating agent's private key over this delegation record. Every delegation record MUST carry this field: it provides independent evidence that the delegator authorized this specific delegation, which the Authorization Server alone cannot attest, and enables non-repudiation. Because the field is REQUIRED, its absence is unambiguous evidence of an invalid record rather than a deployment choice. The signature uses the private key that the record's delegator_id resolves to (see the Key Resolution section of this specification).

An identifier for the Authorization Server that created this delegation record. REQUIRED when as_signature is present, where it identifies the issuer of that signature and enables the verifier to select the correct public key. In single-domain chains where as_signature is omitted, the token's iss claim already identifies the creating AS and this field MAY be omitted.

Signature of the Authorization Server that created this record, over the same field set as delegator_signature. REQUIRED when the record was created by an AS other than the issuer of the token carrying the chain (cross-domain chains), so that the receiving domain can independently verify each foreign hop and hold the creating AS accountable for it. When the record's AS is the token's issuer, the token's own signature already attests to the record and this field MAY be omitted.

section.t: The authorization constraints delegated at a hop are expressed as scope: this is the baseline form, REQUIRED whenever the chain contains more than one record so that scope narrowing along the chain is verifiable by any holder of the token. Deployments that use a structured constraint model additionally carry policy_ref, an opaque reference to the approved constraints. This specification does not define the format, resolution, or comparison of the referenced constraints; narrowing with respect to the delegator's authorization is enforced by the Authorization Server at issuance time () and attested by the record's signatures.
The delegation_timestamp MUST satisfy the following constraints:

ul.li: It MUST be greater than or equal to the delegation_timestamp of the temporally earlier delegation record (the record at the next higher array index), ensuring that timestamps are monotonically non-increasing from index 0 (most recent) to index N (earliest). When the two records were signed by different Authorization Servers (cross-domain chains), this comparison SHOULD tolerate clock skew between the two AS instances, consistent with the freshness window below; a small negative delta between independently clocked hops is not by itself evidence of an invalid chain.

It MUST be within the validity period of the delegator's token at the time of the delegation request (i.e., greater than or equal to the delegator token's iat and less than or equal to the delegator token's exp).

At the time the AS processes the delegation request, the timestamp SHOULD be within an acceptable freshness window relative to the AS's current time. A RECOMMENDED maximum skew is 5 minutes in either direction. Timestamps outside this window SHOULD be rejected to mitigate replay attacks (see ).

section.t: The delegator_signature and, when present, the as_signature MUST be computed over the same set of fields. The signature is a JWS () compact serialization. The JWS payload is a JSON object containing exactly the following fields (omitting OPTIONAL fields that are absent); the payload SHOULD be serialized using the JSON Canonicalization Scheme () so that the same set of fields deterministically produces the same bytes across implementations:

ul.li: scope (if present)
policy_ref (if present)

section.t: Both signature fields MUST be excluded from their respective signature computations. The JWS alg header MUST be set appropriately (e.g., RS256 for AS signatures, ES256 for delegator signatures). The JWS kid header SHOULD be included to facilitate key resolution. The resulting compact JWS string is stored as the value of the respective signature field. When verifying, the verifier decodes the JWS payload and confirms that the decoded JSON object matches the delegation record fields.
The two signatures serve distinct purposes. The delegator_signature, which is REQUIRED on every record, uses the delegating agent's agent-identifier-bound private key and provides:

ul.li: Malicious AS Prevention: A compromised AS cannot unilaterally forge delegations without the delegator's consent;
Non-Repudiation: The delegator cannot deny having authorized the delegation.

section.t: The as_signature uses the creating Authorization Server's signing key. It is REQUIRED only on records created by an AS other than the token's issuer: in single-domain chains, the token-level signature of the issuing AS attests to every record in the chain, so per-record as_signature would duplicate that attestation. In cross-domain chains, it provides the originating AS's witness attestation for each foreign hop, enabling the receiving domain to verify that hop independently of the transcribing AS.

section.title: Key Resolution for Agent Identifiers
section.t: Verification of the delegator_signature (and of the delegatee's key binding) requires the relying party to resolve the agent identifier to a verifiable public key. The resolution mechanism depends on the URI scheme used in the delegator_id or delegatee_id field:
The wit:// scheme used in the examples of this specification has the following syntax:

The authority component identifies the workload identity provider or trust domain (for example, wit://agent-a.example). The first path segment is the agent identifier, conventionally a digest of the agent's public key prefixed by the hash algorithm, for example, wit://agent-a.example/sha256.aaa111...: once the relying party has resolved the authority to a trusted provider, the identifier itself determines which key material it names. Deployments MAY use other agent identifier forms within the same scheme, provided the deployment documents how the identifier resolves to a key. SPIFFE IDs are used with their usual semantics.

ul.li: wit://: The WIT URI is resolved via the workload identity provider's attestation bundle, which contains or references the agent's public key (e.g., via SPIFFE bundle endpoints);
spiffe://: The SPIFFE ID is resolved via the SPIFFE Bundle Endpoint protocol, which provides the agent's X.509-SVID or JWT-SVID containing the public key.

section.t: Implementations SHOULD document the supported URI schemes and their resolution mechanisms in deployment-specific configuration. If the relying party cannot resolve the agent identifier to a trusted public key, it MUST treat the delegator_signature as unverifiable.

section.title: Chain Ordering and Integrity
section.t: The array MUST be ordered from most recent delegation to earliest:

ul.li: Index 0: Most recent delegation (delegator → current token holder)
Index N: Earliest delegation (first agent after human authorization)

section.t: This ordering allows efficient validation starting from the immediate delegator.

The integrity of the array as a whole is provided by the token-level JWT signature: the signature of the AS that issued the token covers the delegation_chain claim in its exact serialized form, so any modification, removal, reordering, or splicing of records invalidates the token. The integrity of each individual record is provided by its signatures: the delegator_signature, which is REQUIRED on every record, covers the hop's delegator, delegatee, scope, and timestamp, and the as_signature, which is REQUIRED on records created by a foreign AS, covers the same fields with the creating AS's key. The hops are bound into a single path by the continuity rule that record[i].delegatee_id MUST equal record[i-1].delegator_id (): both identifiers are covered by the respective records' signatures, so a sequence that combines records from different chains fails either signature verification or the continuity check. A chain that fails these checks is invalid, and the Resource Server MUST reject the token with an invalid_delegation_chain error.

section.title: Ordering Verification Semantics
section.t: The delegation_timestamp field provides ordering evidence for the delegation chain. This section states explicitly which levels of ordering assurance the mechanism provides, and which it does not.

ol.li: Claim-level ordering: Each record's delegation_timestamp is covered by the record's signatures. Monotonicity across the chain (earlier hops carry earlier timestamps) is verifiable by any holder of the token. This is the baseline property this specification provides.

Cross-party attestation: Each hop's ordering evidence carries a signature from a party other than the one whose conduct is at issue at that hop: the delegator_signature from the delegating agent, and, on records that cross a domain boundary, the as_signature from the creating Authorization Server. This corresponds to the independently verifiable property discussed for agent action determinability ().

Commit-time enforcement is out of scope: Ordering evidence in the token establishes when delegations were recorded, not that preconditions still held at the time the delegated operation was executed. This specification does not claim commit-time or execution-time atomicity. A fresh observation of a valid chain is not a guarantee that the world has not changed between delegation and execution. Deployments requiring such guarantees MUST combine this mechanism with execution-time mechanisms (e.g., conditional requests, resource versioning) or a commitment or reservation protocol.

section.t: The boundary above is a property, not a mechanism requirement: token-carried evidence records commitments and does not by itself enforce them at execution time. Whatever execution-time mechanism a deployment adds to this specification, the split of responsibilities remains the same: the chain records who delegated what to whom and when; it does not establish that the delegation's preconditions still held at the moment of execution.

section.title: Delegation Token Exchange
section.t: This section defines how a delegation hop is performed with OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (, grant_type=token-exchange): the delegating agent presents its token together with the delegatee's identity, the delegator-signed delegation proposal, and the requested scope; the AS validates the request and issues a new token for the delegatee carrying the extended delegation_chain. Whether the AS requires user consent before authorizing a delegation hop is AS policy and is out of scope of this specification; the mechanism for obtaining such consent, when required, is likewise out of scope. The figure below shows the flow.
