section.t: Steps (1) and (2) are a standard OAuth flow: Agent A obtains the root authorization from the user, and the resulting token carries no delegation_chain. Steps (6) and (7) are ordinary API usage: Agent B presents the delegated token to the RS, which validates it as defined in . The normative content of this flow is the sequence between them: the delegation request (), the AS validation rules, and token issuance. A step-by-step walkthrough of the steps shown in the figure, including the full HTTP request and response examples, is provided in .

section.title: Delegation Request
section.t: Agent A initiates delegation using OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange . The request includes delegation-specific parameters to identify the delegatee and the delegated authorization constraints. An example request with a WIT-based agent identity and a scope-based delegation is shown in .
This specification defines the following extension parameter for use with Token Exchange requests:

dl.dd: REQUIRED for delegation requests. A URI identifying the agent receiving the delegated authorization. Implementations SHOULD use a WIT URI when workload identity attestation is available, but MAY use other URI schemes (see ). The AS uses this value to bind the issued token to the delegatee's identity and to populate the delegatee_id field in the delegation_chain record.

REQUIRED. A JWS () whose payload is the prospective delegation record for this hop: the JSON object containing every field of the final delegation_chain record except the delegator_signature and as_signature fields. The delegating agent signs the canonical serialization (JCS, ) of that object, the same byte string covered by the record signature computation (), with the private key that the record's delegator_id resolves to. This parameter is the mechanism by which the record's delegator_signature field is produced: upon successful validation, the AS embeds the verified signature into the delegator_signature field of the record it places in the issued token, alongside its own as_signature when the record requires one.

section.t: Relationship to the actor_token parameter: Token Exchange (, Section 4.4) natively supports delegation through the actor_token parameter: when an actor token is provided, the issued token's act claim identifies the actor; when it is not, the issued token identifies the requesting client as the actor. The delegatee_id parameter serves the delegation scenario in which the delegatee does not yet hold a token or a client identity at the AS, the common case for agent-to-agent delegation, where the delegating agent requests a token bound to a delegatee identified by workload identity. A delegation request MUST NOT include both actor_token and delegatee_id; the AS rejects such a request with invalid_request. When delegatee_id is used, this specification overrides the default actor construction of : the issued token's act.sub is set to the delegatee identified by delegatee_id, not to the requesting client, and the token is additionally bound to the delegatee's key as defined in the Token Issuance section.
The standard and extension parameters in the request are:

ul.li: subject_token: Agent A's current access token;
subject_token_type: urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token;

authorization_details (OPTIONAL) (): Carries the delegated constraints in a structured format; the structure is deployment-specific and out of scope of this specification. When present, the constraints MUST be equal to or more restrictive than Agent A's authorization. Deployments that do not use structured constraints convey the delegated constraints via scope alone;
delegatee_id: The agent identifier URI of the delegatee agent (Agent B);
delegation_proposal: The delegator-signed prospective record for this hop (see above);
scope (OPTIONAL): Requested scope for the delegated token, which MUST be a subset of Agent A's scope.

requested_token_type (OPTIONAL): Per , Section 2.1, when this parameter is absent, the issued token type is at the discretion of the Authorization Server, and an opaque access token cannot carry the delegation_chain claim. Implementations using this specification therefore MUST request JWT-format access tokens: the value urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt is REQUIRED for requests in which the delegation_chain claim is expected in the response.

resource (OPTIONAL): The identifier of the target Authorization Server when the delegation crosses a trust domain boundary, as defined in . When present, the AS issues a JWT authorization grant suitable for presentation to the target AS instead of a direct access token. Although permits repeating this parameter, a delegation request MUST NOT include more than one resource value: each delegation hop targets a single trust domain.

audience (OPTIONAL): A well-known or logical name of the target Authorization Server, as an alternative to resource for cross-domain delegation. One of resource or audience is REQUIRED when the delegation targets an agent in a different trust domain.

section.title: AS Validation
section.t: The AS MUST perform the following validations:

ol.li: Token Validity: Verify Agent A's token is valid and not revoked.

Delegation Permission: Confirm the subject token permits delegation to this delegatee. Permission is determined by AS policy, which MAY be expressed through the may_act claim (, Section 4.1) naming the delegatee, a delegation scope, or another deployment-specific mechanism.

Scope Subset: Verify the requested scope is a subset of Agent A's authorized scope (equal to or narrower). Scope expansion is rejected with an invalid_scope error (, Section 5.2); a dedicated error code would not change client behavior here.

Structured Constraints (CONDITIONAL): When the request carries structured constraints, verify that they are equal to or more restrictive than Agent A's authorization. The comparison mechanism is defined by the deployment's constraint model and is out of scope of this specification.
Delegatee Authentication: Validate Agent B's agent identifier (delegatee_id) to confirm the delegatee is authentic and currently active.

Proposal Consistency: Verify the delegation_proposal signature using the public key resolved from the proposed record's delegator_id, confirm that the delegator_id identifies the current holder of the subject token, and confirm that the proposed record is consistent with the request parameters (delegatee_id, scope, and, when present, the constraint references). Reject the request with invalid_request on any mismatch.
Chain Depth: Optionally enforce maximum delegation depth, rejecting the request with delegation_depth_exceeded () when the configured maximum would be exceeded.

Upstream Chain Validation (CONDITIONAL): When the subject token contains a delegation_chain claim, verify the chain's continuity, signatures, and scope narrowing as defined in . If validation fails, reject the request with an invalid_delegation_chain error.

Request Freshness: Reject the delegation request if the request time, as observed by the AS, is outside an acceptable time window. A RECOMMENDED maximum skew is 5 minutes. This prevents replay of previously captured delegation requests.

section.title: Token Issuance
section.t: Upon successful validation, the AS issues a new token for the delegatee with:

ul.li: sub: The original user (unchanged)
act: The delegatee agent's identity, as a single act.sub value without nesting ()
aud: The audience of the subject token, unless the delegation request constrains it (see below)
delegation_chain: Extended with a new record for this hop
scope: The delegated scope (equal to or narrower than the delegator's, as requested)

section.t: Audience handling: the delegated token's aud is inherited from the subject token unless the delegation request constrains it through the resource or audience parameters of . Scope narrowing alone does not narrow audience: a delegatee receiving a narrowed scope still obtains a token valid for the same set of Resource Servers, within that narrowed scope. Deployments in which different delegation hops target different Resource Servers SHOULD constrain the audience at each hop.

When the AS issues the delegated token at the delegator's request, and the delegatee did not authenticate to the AS for this issuance, the token SHOULD be sender-constrained to the delegatee at issuance. The AS resolves the delegatee_id to a public key (see the Key Resolution section of ) and includes a cnf claim () binding the token to the delegatee's key. Two confirmation methods are defined: jkt (the JWK thumbprint defined in ), used with the proof-of-possession protocol of DPoP (), where the Resource Server verifies the DPoP proof JWT accompanying each request; and x5t#S256, used with mutual TLS client certificate binding (). The Resource Server MUST verify presenter possession according to the confirmation method indicated by the cnf claim when it is present. Deployments MAY alternatively require the delegatee itself to authenticate and request the delegated token, in which case standard client authentication and sender-constraining apply.

Note on DPoP binding: binds an issued access token to the key that signed the DPoP proof JWT accompanying the token request, normally the requesting client's key. This specification deviates from that model: the delegated token is bound to the delegatee's key, which presents no proof at the token endpoint, and the AS obtains the delegatee's public key by resolving delegatee_id (see ). The delegating agent's own DPoP proof, when present, authenticates the request; it does not determine the issued token's key binding. Resource Servers verify the delegatee's DPoP proofs against the cnf claim as usual.

section.title: Chain Extension
section.t: When the AS issues a delegated token, it extends the delegation_chain:

The delegator's signature over the new record is produced before the request: the delegating agent signs the prospective record and conveys it in the delegation_proposal parameter of the Token Exchange request (); the AS verifies it as part of request validation and embeds it as the record's delegator_signature. The AS applies its own as_signature to the record when the record is created for a token that will be consumed in another trust domain; within a single trust domain, the token-level signature of the issuing AS suffices. The AS propagates the root_authorization_ref claim from the subject token into the issued token unchanged.

section.title: Root Authorization Reference Propagation
section.t: The root_authorization_ref claim is propagated with the chain: when the AS issues a delegated token within the same trust domain, it copies the claim from the subject token; when the receiving AS of a cross-domain flow issues a local token, it copies the claim from the JWT authorization grant (). Every token in the lineage therefore anchors to the same root authorization, and a verifier can retrieve the original authorization context through the deployment-specific resolution mechanism of the reference (an audit log query, a consent management API, or, in deployments using a structured authorization evidence model, the root token's evidence claim).

section.title: For First Delegation
section.t: If Agent A's token has no delegation_chain (root authorization), the AS creates a new chain with one entry. The following shows an extended first delegation record:

A single-domain, scope-only record would carry only delegator_id, delegatee_id, scope, delegation_timestamp, and delegator_signature, omitting the policy reference and the as_signature, whose role is carried by the token-level signature of the issuing AS.

section.title: For Subsequent Delegations
section.t: If Agent B further delegates to Agent C, the AS prepends a new record. The following shows an extended two-hop chain:

With scope-based delegation only, each record would omit policy_ref. The scope narrowing (cart:read inventory:read to inventory:read) is expressed by each record's scope field and the delegated token's scope claim, and is verifiable by any holder of the token.

section.title: Cross-Domain Delegation
section.t: When delegation hops span multiple trust domains (each with its own Authorization Server), this specification combines the delegation_chain mechanism with the cross-domain transport pattern defined in .
The grant type used for delegation depends on the trust domain boundary:

ul.li: Single-domain delegation: Uses OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (, grant_type=token-exchange) as defined in . Both delegator and delegatee agents trust the same Authorization Server, which can validate the subject token and issue a delegated token directly.

Cross-domain delegation: Combines Token Exchange () at the originating AS with the JWT Bearer Grant (, grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer) at the receiving AS. When agents belong to different trust domains with different Authorization Servers, the originating AS cannot issue a direct access token for the remote domain. Instead, the delegating agent initiates a Token Exchange request at the originating AS, which returns a signed JWT authorization grant. The delegatee agent then presents this grant to its local AS using the JWT Bearer grant type. The receiving AS verifies the grant using the originating AS's public key (obtained via metadata) and issues a local access token.

section.title: Extension of the JWT Authorization Grant
section.t: The JWT authorization grant defined by is extended with two claims. The grant MAY carry the delegation_chain and root_authorization_ref claims defined in . An Authorization Server receiving such a grant MUST process the two claims in accordance with and MUST preserve them verbatim in the access token it issues, as described in . Everything else about the grant, including its issuance, audience binding, and validation, is defined by and is unaffected by this specification. The claims are defined so that they can also be carried by tokens issued without the JWT authorization grant mechanism, for example tokens issued through a direct Token Exchange (); no validation rule in this specification depends on how the token reached its issuer.

section.title: Cross-Domain Delegation Flow
section.t: Consider an agent in Trust Domain A that needs to delegate a subset of its authorization to an agent in Trust Domain B:

figure.artwork: Domain A Domain B User Agent A AS-A Agent B AS-B | | | | | | (1) initial authorization | | | | (root authorization) | | | |-------------->| | | | | | | | | | | (2) Token Exchange | | | | resource=AS-B | | | | delegatee_id=Agent B | | | | delegation_proposal | | | |-------------->| | | | | | | | | | (3) JWT authorization grant | | | | delegation_chain: [A->B] | | | | root_authorization_ref | | | | aud: AS-B | | | | |<--------------| | | | | | | | | | (4) out-of-band transfer | | | |------------------------------>| | | | | | | | | | | (5) Token Exchange | | | |-------------->| | | | | | | | | | (6) validate | | | | | grant and chain | | | | | | | | | (7) access token | | | | chain preserved | | | |<--------------| | | | | |

ol.li: Agent A obtains initial authorization from the user in Trust Domain A (root authorization, no delegation_chain).

Agent A initiates a delegation Token Exchange with AS-A, including the resource parameter set to AS-B's identifier (as defined in ), the delegatee_id parameter identifying Agent B, and the delegation_proposal parameter carrying Agent A's signature over the prospective delegation record. This signals that the delegation targets an agent in Trust Domain B.
AS-A validates the delegation, creates a delegation record carrying its as_signature, and returns a JWT authorization grant containing the delegation_chain and root_authorization_ref claims.
Agent A transfers the JWT authorization grant to Agent B through an out-of-band mechanism (e.g., a secure internal channel).

Agent B presents the JWT authorization grant to AS-B using the JWT Bearer grant type (), as defined in , authenticating itself to AS-B with its client credentials or key material. AS-B verifies that the authenticated presenter is the delegatee named by the most recent delegation record of the grant's delegation_chain.
AS-B validates the JWT grant signature, verifies the delegation_chain (including AS-A's signature on each record), and confirms policy narrowing constraints.

AS-B issues an access token to Agent B for Trust Domain B, preserving the delegation_chain and root_authorization_ref claims from the JWT authorization grant, with act.sub set to Agent B's identifier and, consistent with the Token Issuance section of , the token sender-constrained to Agent B's key.

section.t: Agent B then uses the access token to access resources in Trust Domain B. When Agent B delegates further across another trust domain boundary, the pattern repeats; the second hop is shown in .

section.title: Cross-Domain Trust Requirements
section.t: For cross-domain delegation to function, the following trust requirements MUST be satisfied:

ul.li: AS Trust Relationship: Records created by AS-A for a cross-domain delegation carry as_signature (REQUIRED for records created by an AS other than the token's issuer), so AS-B MUST trust AS-A's signing key to verify those records. This trust relationship is typically established through key exchange or by publishing AS-A's public keys via Authorization Server Metadata ().

delegation_chain Propagation: AS-B MUST propagate the delegation_chain claim from the JWT authorization grant into the access token it issues, so that Resource Servers in Trust Domain B can validate the full delegation lineage.

Presenter verification: AS-B MUST authenticate the client presenting the JWT authorization grant and verify that the authenticated presenter is the delegatee named by the most recent delegation record (record[0].delegatee_id). The originating AS SHOULD sender-constrain the grant to the delegatee's key with a cnf claim (), in which case AS-B verifies the presenter's key against it; where the grant is not constrained, AS-B MUST bind the local access token it issues to the delegatee so that the delegation is usable only by the named delegatee.

Root Authorization Reference Propagation: AS-B MUST propagate the root_authorization_ref claim from the JWT authorization grant, so that Resource Servers in Trust Domain B can anchor the chain to the original user authorization. Deployments using a structured authorization evidence model MAY additionally propagate the root token's evidence claim, subject to data minimization policies, privacy regulations, or trust agreements between domains; when it is not propagated, the root_authorization_ref value remains the anchor, resolvable through deployment-specific back-channel mechanisms.

Constraint Enforcement: AS-B MUST enforce that the delegated scope is equal to or narrower than the scope in the JWT authorization grant; scope expansion across domain boundaries is not permitted. When the policy_ref field is present, AS-B relies on the originating AS's issuance-time attestation of the referenced constraints (carried in the record's as_signature), or resolves and compares the references according to its deployment-specific constraint model.

section.title: Multi-Domain Chain Extension
section.t: When a delegation chain spans multiple domains, each domain's AS may add delegation records to the chain. The cross-domain transport uses the identity chaining pattern (Token Exchange + JWT Bearer Grant) at each domain boundary, while the delegation_chain accumulates records from all domains.
A second hop, from Agent B in Trust Domain B to an agent in Trust Domain C, proceeds symmetrically:

figure.artwork: Domain B Domain C Agent B AS-B Agent C AS-C RS-C | | | | | | (1) Token Exchange | | | | resource=AS-C | | | | delegation_proposal | | | |------------->| | | | | | | | | | (2) JWT authorization grant | | | | chain: [B->C, A->B] | | | | root_authorization_ref | | | |<-------------| | | | | | | | | | (3) out-of-band transfer | | | |---------------------------->| | | | | | | | | | | (4) Token Exchange | | | |------------->| | | | | | | | | | | (5) validate | | | | | grant and chain | | | | | | | | (6) access token | | | | chain preserved | | | |<-------------| | | | | | | | | | (7) API request | | | |---------------------------->| | | | | | | | | | (8) validate chain | | | | and root anchor | | | | |

ol.li: Agent B initiates a delegation Token Exchange with AS-B, with the resource parameter set to AS-C's identifier, the delegatee_id parameter identifying Agent C, and the delegation_proposal parameter carrying Agent B's signature over the prospective delegation record.

AS-B validates the delegation, creates the delegation record for this hop carrying its as_signature, and returns a JWT authorization grant for AS-C whose delegation_chain contains both records (AS-A's record preserved verbatim) and whose root_authorization_ref is propagated from the original authorization.
Agent B transfers the JWT authorization grant to Agent C through an out-of-band mechanism.

Agent C presents the JWT authorization grant to AS-C using the JWT Bearer grant type (), authenticating itself to AS-C; AS-C verifies that the authenticated presenter is the delegatee named by the most recent delegation record of the grant's delegation_chain.

AS-C validates the JWT grant signature and the full delegation_chain, including the as_signature on each record created by a foreign AS (here, both AS-A's and AS-B's records), and confirms scope narrowing across the whole chain.

AS-C issues Agent C a local access token preserving the delegation_chain and root_authorization_ref claims verbatim, with act.sub set to Agent C's identifier and the token sender-constrained to Agent C's key.
Agent C presents the access token to RS-C.
RS-C validates the delegation_chain as defined in and enforces the resulting decision.

section.t: Resource Servers validating a cross-domain delegation chain MUST:

ul.li: Verify the delegator_signature on each delegation record, and the as_signature on each record that carries one, using the signing key of the AS identified by that record's as_id field (which may differ across records);
Verify trust relationships between all ASes referenced in the chain;
Verify chain continuity and scope narrowing across domain boundaries;

section.title: Claims Transcription for Delegation
section.t: Section 2.5 of describes Claims Transcription (the process by which Authorization Servers add, change, or remove claims during cross-domain token flows) but leaves the representation of transcribed claims undefined. The delegation_chain claim provides one such representation: when delegation crosses a trust domain boundary, each delegation record captures the transcribed authorization constraints (scope, and when present policy_ref), the identity mapping (delegator and delegatee identifiers), and the cryptographic evidence of the delegating agent (delegator_signature) and of the originating AS that created the record (as_signature).

This enables the receiving domain's AS (AS-B) to verify what claims were transcribed, who authorized the transcription, and under what constraints, which addresses the representation gap left by the base identity chaining specification. AS-B SHOULD validate the delegation_chain records from AS-A as part of its Claims Transcription processing before issuing a local access token. In this processing, AS-B preserves the upstream records verbatim: it MUST NOT alter, re-sign, or replace them, and each record's as_id and as_signature remain those of the originating AS; AS-B's own attestation of the transcribed claims is the signature on the local access token it issues.

section.title: Resource Server Validation
section.t: Resource Servers validate the delegation_chain as follows:

section.title: Signature Verification
section.t: For each record in the chain, the Resource Server MUST verify the delegator_signature using the public key of the delegating agent identified by the record's delegator_id field, resolved as described in . A record without a delegator_signature, or with a delegator_signature that does not verify, makes the delegation_chain invalid, and the Resource Server MUST reject the token.

When a record was created by an AS other than the AS that issued the token, the record MUST carry an as_signature, and the Resource Server MUST verify it using the public key of the AS identified by the record's as_id field. In single-domain chains, every record is created by the token's issuer, as_id matches the token's iss claim, and the as_signature is typically omitted: the token-level JWT signature already attests to every record in the chain. In cross-domain chains, different records may carry different as_id values, and the Resource Server MUST select the corresponding AS public key for each record. The Resource Server does not need to verify that upstream records' as_id values match the current token's iss claim; the as_id is used solely to select the correct public key for as_signature verification.
Signature verification ensures:

ul.li: The delegation was authorized by the delegating agent;
The delegation was witnessed by the originating AS, for records that carry an as_signature;
The record has not been tampered with.

section.title: Root Authorization Anchor
section.t: Every token that carries a delegation_chain claim also carries a root_authorization_ref claim, which points to the original authorization event in which the user authorized the root agent. The last record in the chain (highest index) represents the earliest delegation, and its delegator_id identifies the root agent. The authorization of the root agent by the user is not a delegation record and is not represented in the chain; it is anchored by the root_authorization_ref claim.

The Resource Server SHOULD verify the root authorization anchor. Since the RS typically observes only the delegated token, it does not have direct access to the original authorization event. The root_authorization_ref value is opaque to this specification; its resolution and validation are deployment-specific. Verification can be performed through one or more of the following means:

ul.li: Resolving the root_authorization_ref through deployment-specific mechanisms, for example to a consent record or an audit log entry, and confirming that the referenced authorization event is valid and has not been revoked;
Using token introspection () to confirm that the root agent (identified by the delegator_id of the last chain record) holds a valid, non-revoked root authorization issued by a trusted AS;

Relying on the structural integrity of the delegation_chain itself: the AS that issued the delegated token has already verified the upstream chain, and the token-level JWT signature covers the entire delegation_chain array, binding the issuance attestation to the token as a whole.

section.t: If the RS cannot establish confidence in the root authorization anchor through any available mechanism, it SHOULD reject the request.

section.title: Delegator and AS Attestations
section.t: The two signatures serve distinct purposes and are evaluated independently. The delegator_signature is present on every record: it is the delegating agent's own attestation of the delegation, and it is what prevents a malicious or compromised AS from forging a delegation the delegating agent never made. The as_signature, when present, is the originating AS's attestation that it processed the delegation request, validated the upstream chain, and created the record; it is REQUIRED on records created by an AS other than the AS that issued the token.

ul.li: Delegator Signature: Confirms the delegating agent explicitly authorized this delegation, providing non-repudiation of each hop and protection against record forgery by a compromised AS;
AS Signature: Confirms the originating AS witnessed the delegation and created the record, providing an independent attestation for hops that cross a trust domain boundary.

section.t: Because the delegator_signature is mandatory, the Resource Server never relies on the issuing AS as the sole attester of a delegation. Every hop carries the delegating agent's own signature, and the AS attestation supplements it exactly where the record's creator is not the token's issuer.

section.title: Agent Identifier Status Validation
section.t: The Resource Server SHOULD verify the current status of all agent identifiers referenced in the delegation_chain. The verification mechanism depends on the identifier scheme:

ul.li: WIT URIs (wit://, spiffe://): Check WIT revocation lists or status endpoints, validate expiration timestamps, or query the issuing identity provider for current status.

section.t: If any agent identifier in the chain has been revoked or its associated key material has expired, the entire delegation_chain MUST be considered invalid, even if individual records remain cryptographically valid.

section.title: Chain Continuity
section.t: Verify the chain is continuous:

ul.li: For each record at index i (where i > 0), record[i].delegatee_id MUST equal record[i-1].delegator_id, ensuring that the agent who received authorization in one hop is the same agent that delegates in the next hop;
The delegatee_id of the most recent delegation record (index 0) matches the token's act.sub, and the act claim carries no nested act claim ();

Timestamps are in descending order: for every record at index i (where i > 0), record[i].delegation_timestamp MUST be less than or equal to record[i-1].delegation_timestamp (two hops within the same second are permitted). When adjacent records carry different as_id values, the verifier SHOULD allow clock skew between the two Authorization Servers (consistent with the freshness window recommended in ) before rejecting on timestamp ordering alone.

section.title: Scope and Constraint Validation
section.t: Authorization constraints MUST NOT expand along the chain. The constraint data visible to the Resource Server is the per-record scope field and the token's own scope claim; the root boundary (the earliest hop's scope versus the delegator's originally authorized scope) was enforced by the Authorization Server at issuance time and is attested by the record signatures.

ul.li: Scope narrowing (MUST): For every record at index i > 0, the set of scope values in record[i].scope MUST be a subset of the set of scope values in record[i+1].scope. The scope of the presented token MUST be a subset of record[0].scope and MUST cover the requested operation. Scope expansion at any hop, or a missing scope field on a multi-record chain, invalidates the chain: the Resource Server MUST reject the token with an invalid_delegation_chain error.

Structured constraints (CONDITIONAL): When policy_ref is present, the Resource Server relies on the Authorization Server's issuance-time validation of the referenced constraints, attested by as_signature when present and by the token-level signature otherwise. A Resource Server that is able to resolve the reference according to its deployment-specific constraint model MAY additionally evaluate the referenced constraints for the requested operation.

section.t: When a Resource Server rejects a request because delegation chain validation fails, it responds with HTTP 403 (Forbidden) carrying the error code invalid_delegation_chain, following the error signaling conventions of , Section 3: a WWW-Authenticate header field for bearer token presentation, or the API's own error response body where the API defines one. The error code is the same one registered for token endpoint use in ; its meaning at the Resource Server is specific to delegation chain validation.

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: The security considerations of and apply to this specification. The following considerations follow the guidelines in .

section.title: Threat Model
section.t: This section describes the threat model underlying the delegation_chain mechanism and the security properties it provides.

ul.li: The Authorization Server (AS) is trusted to correctly validate delegation requests, enforce policy narrowing, and sign delegation records with its private key. The AS is the central trust anchor for the delegation chain.

The human principal (end user) is trusted to make informed authorization decisions. Whether and how the Authorization Server obtains the user's consent for a delegation is AS policy and is out of scope of this specification.
A malicious delegatee agent may attempt to present a token with a forged or truncated delegation_chain to claim authorization it does not possess.
A malicious delegator agent may attempt to delegate more authorization than it was granted (privilege escalation), or may deny having authorized a delegation (repudiation).

A compromised AS may attempt to forge delegation records without the delegator's consent. The mandatory delegator_signature on every record mitigates this threat: a forged record does not verify against the delegating agent's key. On records created by a foreign AS, the as_signature provides the additional attestation of the AS that created the record.
A network attacker may attempt to intercept or modify delegation records in transit. Standard TLS protections apply to all protocol messages.

A token thief may attempt to steal a delegated access token (e.g., by compromising an agent's storage, intercepting a token in transit, or exploiting a side-channel) and present it to a Resource Server as if it were the legitimate delegatee. The thief may also attempt to replay a previously captured delegation request to obtain a new token.

A credential thief may attempt to steal an agent's workload identity credentials (e.g., WIT signing key, SPIFFE SVID, or client attestation key material) and impersonate the agent to obtain unauthorized delegations from the AS. This threat is particularly severe in multi-hop chains, where a single compromised agent identity can be used to initiate new delegation paths.

section.t: Security Objectives: The delegation_chain claim provides the following security properties:

ul.li: Integrity: Each delegation record is cryptographically signed by the delegator, and by the AS that created it when the record crosses a trust domain boundary, preventing undetected modification.
Non-repudiation: The delegator_signature on every record provides independent evidence that the delegation was explicitly authorized by the delegator.

Scope compliance: Mandatory scope narrowing at each hop prevents privilege escalation through the chain. When the policy_ref field is present, the referenced constraints provide additional fine-grained enforcement attested at issuance time.
Auditability: The complete chain from the current actor back to the original human principal enables end-to-end audit trail reconstruction.

section.title: Privilege Escalation Prevention
section.t: The AS MUST ensure that delegation cannot expand privileges:

ul.li: Delegated scope MUST be a subset of (equal to or narrower than) delegator's scope;
Delegation depth MAY be limited;
Certain scopes MAY be marked non-delegatable.

section.title: Chain Integrity
section.t: Chain integrity is ensured jointly by the token-level JWT signature, which covers the entire delegation_chain claim in its exact serialized form, and by the per-record delegator_signature, which is REQUIRED on every record. Records created by an AS other than the token's issuer additionally carry that AS's as_signature. These mechanisms enforce chain integrity through the following properties:

ul.li: Forgery prevention: Neither a malicious agent nor a compromised AS can forge a delegation record: creating a valid record requires the delegating agent's signature over the record's fields, and a record created by a foreign AS additionally requires that AS's as_signature.

Tamper detection: Agents cannot modify existing records because any change to the signed fields (including delegator_id, delegatee_id, delegation_timestamp, scope, and policy_ref) invalidates the record's delegator_signature, the as_signature when present, and the token-level JWT signature.

Record removal detection: Agents cannot remove records from the chain because the token-level JWT signature covers the entire delegation_chain claim as a single unit; any modification to the array length or contents invalidates the token signature.
Reorder detection: Agents cannot reorder records because the token-level JWT signature covers the delegation_chain array in its exact serialized form; any reordering invalidates the token signature.

section.t: The four properties above hold for every deployment: the delegator_signature is mandatory on every record, and the token-level signature covers the array as a whole. In single-domain deployments, records typically omit the as_signature, since the token issuer attests to every record through the token-level signature. In cross-domain deployments, the as_signature on foreign records adds independent per-hop attestation that survives token re-issuance.

Additionally, the Resource Server SHOULD verify that the delegation_timestamp on each record falls within a reasonable window relative to the token's iat (issued-at) claim. Timestamps that significantly predate the token's issuance or fall in the future may indicate a manipulated or replayed delegation record.

section.title: Chain Stripping Prevention
section.t: A malicious agent may attempt to present a token with a truncated or empty delegation_chain to hide intermediate delegation hops. For example, an agent holding a token whose chain represents A→B→C (two records: C←B and B←A) could attempt to present only the most recent record [C←B] or an empty chain, thereby concealing the earlier hops from the Resource Server.
This attack is prevented by the following mechanisms:

ul.li: Token-level signature: The AS signs the entire access token (including the delegation_chain claim) using its private key. Any modification to the delegation_chain claim (including removal of records or replacement with a shorter chain) invalidates the token's signature. The Resource Server MUST reject tokens whose signature does not verify.

section.t: For opaque (non-JWT) access tokens, the Resource Server MUST use token introspection () to retrieve the authoritative delegation_chain from the AS, rather than trusting any client-supplied chain data.

section.title: Reordering and Splicing Attacks
section.t: Beyond removing records, an attacker holding tokens from multiple delegations may attempt to reorder the records of a chain, or to splice records from two different chains into a new sequence that was never issued by any AS (for example, prefixing a chain with a permissive first hop taken from another user's chain).

ul.li: Reordering: The token-level JWT signature covers the array in its exact serialized form, so any reordering invalidates it. Independently, the continuity rule of fails for a reordered sequence: each record binds its delegator_id and delegatee_id under the delegator's signature, so an attacker cannot rewire a record to a different predecessor or successor.

Splicing: A spliced sequence combines records that were each individually signed, but into a path that never existed. The token-level signature rejects it outright. If a splice is re-embedded into a newly issued token, which only a malicious or compromised AS can do, the continuity check fails at the splice point unless the AS can also obtain a genuine delegator_signature binding the two chains, and a token that embeds a broken chain is attributable to the AS that issued it.

section.t: The ordering assurance levels follow : claim-level ordering prevents forgery of a hop's timestamp; cross-party attestation prevents a delegating agent from forging the ordering evidence of its own hop; commit-time enforcement is not provided by this specification and is out of scope. Implementations MUST NOT rely on chain validation in place of execution-time checks.

section.title: Policy Reference Substitution
section.t: When policy_ref is used, an attacker who can modify a record might substitute the reference to point to different (broader) constraints. This attack is prevented by the record's signatures: the reference is part of the signed field set, so any substitution invalidates the record's delegator_signature, the as_signature when present, and the token-level signature.

This specification does not define end-to-end verification of the referenced constraints. A Resource Server that requires such verification resolves the reference according to its deployment-specific constraint model, or relies on the Authorization Server's issuance-time validation attested by the record signatures.

section.title: Confidentiality of Delegation Records
section.t: A delegation chain may contain privacy-sensitive information and, to prevent disclosure to unintended parties, should only be transmitted over encrypted channels, such as Transport Layer Security (TLS). All claims in a signed but unencrypted JWT (JWS, ) are Base64URL-encoded and readable by any party that obtains the token, including the full delegation topology (all agent identities), policy references (policy_ref), and the authorization event reference (root_authorization_ref).

In cases where it is desirable to prevent disclosure of delegation records to unintended parties, the JWT should be encrypted using JWE () with nested JWT processing (JWE(JWS(payload))), so that only the intended Resource Server can read the delegation chain contents. In cross-domain deployments, JWE encryption should be used to prevent downstream domains from reading upstream delegation records.

Deployments should determine the minimum amount of information necessary for delegation validation and include only such claims in delegation records. The constraints referenced by policy_ref should be scoped to the specific operations being delegated. Agent identifiers (delegator_id, delegatee_id) can be pseudonymous WIT or SPIFFE URIs rather than human-readable names, as described in Section 6.3.1 of the OAuth Assertion Framework ().
The RECOMMENDED short token lifetime (5 to 15 minutes, see ) limits the exposure window of any leaked delegation records.

section.title: Token Protection
section.t: Delegated tokens are subject to replay and theft attacks. The following mitigations address both threats.
Sender-constrained tokens: Implementations SHOULD bind issued access tokens to the delegatee's key material using one of the following mechanisms:

ul.li: DPoP (): The delegatee presents a proof-of-possession JWT alongside the access token. The Resource Server verifies that the DPoP proof's jkt thumbprint matches the key binding in the access token.

Mutual TLS (mTLS, ): The delegatee authenticates using a client certificate; the access token carries an x5t#S256 thumbprint of the certificate, and the certificate is bound to the delegatee_id in the delegation record.

section.t: When the AS binds the delegated token to the delegatee's key at issuance through a cnf claim (), as defined in the Token Issuance section of , the Resource Server verifies presenter possession according to the confirmation method. When sender-constrained tokens are not used, the delegatee_id field alone provides only application-level binding. Deployments that accept this weaker binding SHOULD compensate with shorter token lifetimes and network-level controls.
Delegation request replay: An attacker replays a captured Token Exchange request to the AS to obtain a new delegated token. Mitigations include:

ul.li: Sender-constrained tokens on the delegating agent's access token (e.g., DPoP () or mutual TLS) ensure that a replayed request from a different endpoint fails client authentication at the AS;
TLS protects all protocol messages from on-path capture.

section.t: Token replay and theft: An attacker presents a stolen delegated token to a Resource Server. Mitigations include:

ul.li: Presenter verification: The Resource Server MUST verify that the presenter's authenticated identity matches delegatee_id of the most recent delegation record (index 0);
Revocation propagation: When theft is detected, the AS SHOULD revoke the compromised delegation hop, invalidating all downstream tokens (see ).

section.t: Implementations SHOULD use sender-constrained tokens for both the delegation request and the issued delegated token, especially in multi-hop chains where a stolen token could grant access across multiple trust boundaries. The delegation_chain claim additionally enables post-incident forensic analysis by identifying the agents and timestamps at each hop.

section.title: Delegation Depth Limits
section.t: Implementations SHOULD enforce maximum delegation depth to:

ul.li: Prevent unbounded delegation chains;
Limit token size growth;
Simplify validation.

section.t: A RECOMMENDED default maximum depth is 5 hops.

When a delegation request would exceed the configured maximum depth, the AS MUST reject the request with an OAuth 2.0 error response using the error code delegation_depth_exceeded and a human-readable error_description indicating the maximum delegation depth has been reached. If a Resource Server receives a token whose delegation_chain length exceeds its locally configured maximum depth, it SHOULD reject the request regardless of signature validity, as excessively deep chains may indicate a misconfigured or malicious delegation path.

Implementers should consider the impact of delegation chain depth on token size. Each delegation record typically adds 500 to 1000 bytes to the token payload, including one or two JWS signatures (approximately 200 bytes each for ES256) and, when present, one policy reference per record. A 5-hop delegation chain may therefore add 2.5 to 5 KB to the access token. This can cause issues with:

ul.li: HTTP header size limits (commonly 8 KB in default proxy configurations);
TLS record size constraints;
Client and server memory consumption during token parsing.

section.t: To mitigate token size growth, implementations MAY use one or more of the following strategies:

ul.li: Short-lived tokens with introspection: Issue access tokens with short expiration and rely on token introspection () to retrieve the delegation_chain on demand;
Policy references: Carry structured constraints by reference (policy_ref) rather than embedding constraint content in the delegation records, as this specification defines.

section.title: Cross-Domain Trust
section.t: When delegation chains span multiple trust domains, additional security considerations apply:

ul.li: AS Key Trust and Record Attribution: Resource Servers in each trust domain must be able to verify as_signature on delegation records issued by Authorization Servers in other trust domains. Delegation records created by an AS in another trust domain MUST carry that AS's as_signature, and Resource Servers MUST verify it. Each delegation record carries an as_id field that identifies the AS that created it, enabling the Resource Server to select the correct public key for signature verification. When delegation records cross a domain boundary, the receiving AS preserves the upstream records with their original as_id and as_signature values intact. To obtain the public key for a given as_id, the Resource Server uses Authorization Server Metadata (), a shared trust framework, or deployment-specific key exchange. When the receiving AS adds new delegation records to the chain, it signs them with its own signing key and sets as_id to its own identifier. Cross-domain key trust relationships may be established through key exchange agreements, published JWKS endpoints (), or a shared trust framework. Failure to properly verify cross-domain AS signatures may allow forged delegation records to be accepted.

Claim Semantics Across Domains: Claims such as sub, scope, and policy identifiers may have different semantics across trust domains. Implementations MUST ensure that claim interpretation is consistent or explicitly mapped at each domain boundary, following the claims transcription guidance in .

Revocation Propagation: When the root authorization or any intermediate delegation is revoked, all downstream delegated tokens SHOULD be invalidated. Within a single trust domain, the AS can directly revoke delegated tokens. Across trust domains, implementations SHOULD mitigate the risk of stale delegated tokens through one or more of the following approaches: issuing short-lived delegated tokens to minimize the revocation window, implementing back-channel revocation notifications between ASes (e.g., using Token Revocation or a proprietary notification mechanism), or requiring Resource Servers in the downstream domain to perform token introspection () before accepting delegated tokens.

Lateral Movement: An attacker who compromises an agent in one trust domain may attempt to use the delegation chain to move laterally to other trust domains. Cross-domain delegation SHOULD be restricted by policy to only the trust domains explicitly authorized by the original user consent.

section.title: Delegation Revocation
section.t: Revocation of delegated authorization is a critical security operation. This section defines the revocation semantics for delegation chains.

ul.li: Root revocation: When the original user revokes the root authorization (the token without a delegation_chain), all downstream delegated tokens derived from that root authorization MUST be considered invalid. Resource Servers validating a delegation chain MUST verify that the root authorization remains valid, either by checking the root token's status directly or by using token introspection () on the root token.

Intermediate hop revocation: When a delegating agent revokes a specific delegation hop (e.g., Agent A revokes its delegation to Agent B), all tokens derived from that delegation (including further downstream delegations such as Agent B to Agent C to Agent D) MUST be considered invalid. Resource Servers SHOULD verify that no delegation record in the chain has been revoked. Within a single trust domain, this can be achieved by introspecting the presented token (): the AS evaluates the revocation status of each delegation hop of the chain as part of the introspection response, since only the presented token is available to the Resource Server. In cross-domain or high-throughput deployments, performing per-hop introspection may be impractical; in such cases, Resource Servers MAY rely on short token lifetimes combined with back-channel revocation notifications to limit the window during which a revoked delegation remains effective.

Delegatee token revocation: When a delegatee agent's own token is revoked, only that specific token is affected. The delegation chain record itself remains valid for audit purposes, but the delegatee can no longer use the delegated authorization.

section.t: Revocation Detection Mechanisms: Resource Servers and downstream Authorization Servers MUST implement at least one of the following mechanisms to detect delegation revocation:

ul.li: Short-lived tokens: Issue delegated tokens with short expiration times (e.g., 5 to 15 minutes) to limit the window during which a revoked delegation remains effective;
Token introspection: Perform token introspection () on each token in the delegation chain before accepting the delegated authorization, confirming that no token has been revoked;

Back-channel revocation notifications: Subscribe to revocation events from upstream Authorization Servers using Token Revocation () or a proprietary notification mechanism, enabling proactive invalidation of downstream delegated tokens.

section.title: Privacy Considerations
section.t: In addition to the privacy considerations outlined in and , the following privacy considerations apply to the delegation_chain mechanism defined in this specification.

section.title: Data Minimization
section.t: The delegation_chain claim carries identity and authorization information about the original user, all intermediate agents, and the delegation policies. As the chain grows with each hop, the amount of information embedded in the token increases. Implementations should apply data minimization principles:

ul.li: The constraints referenced by policy_ref should be scoped to the specific operations being delegated, not include broader context about the user's overall authorization.
Agent identifiers (delegator_id, delegatee_id) should be pseudonymous where possible, avoiding direct exposure of personally identifiable information.

section.title: Cross-Domain Information Leakage
section.t: When delegation chains cross trust domain boundaries, the delegation_chain claim propagates user and agent identity information from the originating domain to downstream domains. This creates the following privacy risks:

ul.li: The sub claim reveals the original user's identity in the originating domain to all downstream domains. Implementations should consider identifier mapping or pairwise pseudonymous identifiers, following the claims transcription guidance in .

The root_authorization_ref claim is opaque in this specification, but in deployments where it is resolvable, resolution may expose details of the original consent interaction (e.g., displayed content, session context, channel). ASes should limit who may resolve the reference and should minimize the information returned by resolution.
The complete delegation chain reveals the full topology of agent relationships, which may be sensitive in competitive or multi-tenant environments.

section.title: User Consent Transparency
section.t: Whether an Authorization Server requires user consent before authorizing a delegation hop is AS policy and is out of scope of this specification (). Deployments that do require consent should ensure that the consent interaction clearly communicates:

ul.li: The identity of the delegatee agent receiving the delegation;
The specific operations being delegated;
Whether the delegation crosses trust domain boundaries;
The user's ability to revoke the delegation at any time.

section.t: This specification registers the following claims in the "JSON Web Token Claims" registry:

dl.dd: An ordered array of delegation records tracing agent-to-agent authorization transfers, each record signed by the delegating agent and, for records created by an Authorization Server other than the token's issuer, by that Authorization Server, enabling end-to-end validation of delegation lineage.
An opaque reference to the original user authorization event from which a delegation chain derives, carried in every token that contains a delegation_chain claim.

section.title: Complete Multi-Hop Example
section.t: The following shows the token held by Agent C after two delegation hops (User → Agent A → Agent B → Agent C), using WIT-based identifiers, scope-based delegation, and the sender-constraining cnf claim of :
This token shows:

ul.li: Original user: user_12345
Current actor: Agent C
Delegation path: Agent A → Agent B → Agent C
A flat act claim naming only the current delegatee: the actor lineage lives in delegation_chain, not in nested act claims ()
Progressive scope narrowing: cart:read inventory:read → inventory:read, expressed in both the token's scope claim and each record's scope field
A token-level root_authorization_ref claim anchoring the chain to the original user authorization
Sender-constraining cnf claim binding the token to Agent C's key

section.t: The root_authorization_ref and policy_ref values are opaque references: the former points to the original user authorization event, the latter to the structured authorization constraints approved for that hop. Neither is resolved or interpreted by this specification. root_authorization_ref is REQUIRED whenever delegation_chain is present; policy_ref MAY be omitted, in which case the delegated authorization is expressed solely by scope.

This example is single-domain: both records were created by the AS that issued the token, so the as_signature fields are optional attestations; in a cross-domain token, records created by a foreign AS carry a REQUIRED as_signature from that AS (). The delegator_signature on each record is computed over the JCS () canonical serialization of the record's signed field set; the canonical form and a worked example are given in .

section.title: Step-by-Step Delegation Token Exchange Walkthrough (Informative)
section.t: This appendix walks through the seven steps of the flow in , including the full HTTP request example. It is informative; the normative requirements are stated in the referenced sections.
Steps 1-2, Initial authorization: Agent A obtains authorization from the user through a standard OAuth flow. The resulting token is the root authorization and carries no delegation_chain.

Step 3, Delegation request: Agent A sends a Token Exchange request to the token endpoint. The following example shows a delegation request with a WIT-based agent identity and a scope-based delegation:

figure.artwork:
POST /token HTTP/1.1 Host: as.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Agrant-type%3Atoken-exchange &subject_token=eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiJ9... &subject_token_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Atoken-type%3Aaccess_token &requested_token_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Atoken-type%3Ajwt &scope=cart%3Aread &delegatee_id=wit%3A%2F%2Fagent-b.example%2Fsha256.bbb222... &delegation_proposal=eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiJ9..MEYCIQD1...

section.t: The delegation_proposal parameter carries the delegator-signed prospective record, whose signature is the same byte string that becomes the record's delegator_signature (). Deployments using structured constraints would additionally carry them via authorization_details; the structure is deployment-specific and out of scope of this specification.

Step 4, Validation: The AS performs the validations listed in (token validity, delegation permission, scope subset, delegatee authentication, proposal consistency, chain depth, upstream chain validation, request freshness).

Step 5, Token issuance: The AS issues the delegated token for Agent B, with sub unchanged, act set to Agent B's identity, the delegation_chain extended with a new record for this hop, the token-level root_authorization_ref claim propagated from the subject token, and reduced scope.
Step 5.5, Transfer: Agent A delivers the delegated token to Agent B through an out-of-band mechanism (e.g., a secure internal channel).
Steps 6-7, API request and validation: Agent B uses the delegated token to access the Resource Server. The RS validates the token and verifies the delegation_chain as defined in .

section.title: Validation Checklist
section.t: This appendix provides a condensed checklist for implementers. The normative requirements are specified in and ; this checklist is informative only.

Every token that carries a delegation_chain claim also carries the token-level root_authorization_ref claim. Each delegation record carries a REQUIRED delegator_signature from the delegating agent; records created by an Authorization Server other than the token's issuer additionally carry that AS's as_signature.

ul.li: iss: Authorization Server identifier
sub: original user (preserved from root)
act.sub: delegatee agent identifier
scope: delegated scope (equal to or narrower than the delegator's)
root_authorization_ref: reference to the original user authorization event (REQUIRED with delegation_chain)
delegation_chain: accumulated delegation records
cnf: delegatee key binding, when the token is sender-constrained ()
Token signed by AS private key

ol.li: Verify token-level JWT signature against iss
Verify presenter possession when a cnf claim is present, according to the confirmation method (MUST)
Verify the delegator_signature on every delegation record, using the delegating agent's key resolved from its delegator_id (MUST; reject with invalid_delegation_chain if missing or invalid)
Verify the as_signature on records created by an AS other than the token's issuer, using the key of the AS identified by the record's as_id (MUST)
Check chain continuity: record[i].delegatee_id == record[i-1].delegator_id
Check that the root_authorization_ref claim is present (MUST) and verify the root authorization anchor as described in
Check act.sub == record[0].delegatee_id, and that act carries no nested act claim ()
Check timestamp ordering (descending, within validity)

Check scope narrowing (MUST): record[i].scope is a subset of record[i+1].scope for every i > 0, and the token's scope claim is a subset of record[0].scope; treat policy_ref as opaque (narrowing of structured constraints is attested by the AS at issuance time, not verified by the RS)
Check agent identifier status (revocation / expiration)

section.t: Per-hop signing benefits: independent non-repudiation per delegator, flexible per-hop revocation, incremental chain updates, and discrete audit events.

section.title: Changes from -01 (Informative)
section.t: The following substantive changes were made between draft-liu-oauth-chain-delegation-01 and this document:

ul.li: Structured constraints carried by reference: The inline delegated_policy object (previously carrying Rego policy content) is replaced by the opaque policy_ref field. The structure and resolution of referenced constraints are deployment-specific and out of scope; the Resource Server treats the value as opaque, and any format defined by a deployment MUST NOT expand the delegator's authorization.

Two-level scope narrowing: The Authorization Server enforces the narrowing boundary at issuance time (requested scope within delegator scope, rejected with the existing invalid_scope error); the Resource Server verifies only chain-visible data (per-record scope subsets and the token scope claim within record[0].scope). scope is REQUIRED on records of multi-record chains. The policy_expansion_detected error code registration was removed as redundant.

Token-to-delegatee key binding: At issuance, the AS resolves the delegatee_id to a public key and binds the delegated token to it with a cnf claim (); the Resource Server MUST verify presenter possession when cnf is present.

root_authorization_ref as a token-level claim: The per-record root_evidence_ref field of -01 is replaced by a token-level claim, renamed root_authorization_ref, REQUIRED in every token that carries a delegation_chain. The hop in which the user authorized the root agent is not a delegation record; the claim anchors the chain to that authorization event.
Field rename: The record field delegated_policy_ref of -01 is renamed policy_ref.

Mandatory delegator signature and scoped AS attestation: The delegator_signature is REQUIRED on every record, and the delegation_proposal request parameter is REQUIRED, so a record without a valid delegator signature is unambiguously invalid. The as_signature is REQUIRED only when the record was created by an AS other than the token's issuer, with as_id REQUIRED whenever as_signature is present. The signed field set is narrowed to delegator_id, delegatee_id, as_id, delegation_timestamp, scope, and, when present, policy_ref.

Removal of the hash chain, operation_summary, and chain by reference: The prev_record_hash field and the JCS hash-chaining of records are removed; chain integrity now rests on the token-level signature, the per-record signatures, and the continuity rule. The operation_summary field is removed for data minimization. The delegation_chain_ref claim and the chain-by-reference mechanism are removed.

User interaction mechanism removed: The interaction branch of the delegation Token Exchange flow (the delegation_interaction_required and delegation_interaction_pending errors, interaction_uri, polling, and the interaction_callback_uri parameter) is removed along with its IANA registrations. Whether the AS requires user consent before authorizing a delegation hop is AS policy and is out of scope of this specification.
Test vectors: The informative test vector now covers the JCS () canonicalization of the record's signed field set, over which both signatures are computed.

RFC 8693 alignment: A delegation request MUST NOT combine delegatee_id with actor_token, and the issued token's act claim is pinned to a single act.sub value without nesting, the actor lineage being carried by delegation_chain. The relationship to the may_act claim and the audience semantics of the delegated token are specified.

Delegator signature production and cross-domain presenter verification: The delegation_proposal request parameter is defined as the mechanism by which the delegator's signature over the prospective delegation record is conveyed to the AS; the DPoP binding deviation of the delegated token, and the requirement that the receiving AS verify the presenter of a cross-domain JWT authorization grant against the chain's current delegatee, are stated.

Positioning against ID-JAG: The introduction maps this specification onto the delegation requirements that the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant explicitly leaves open (actor_token processing, authorization propagation across downstream hops, and agent-to-agent delegation), and states where the two specifications compose; the cross-domain section defines the extension of the JWT authorization grant with the delegation_chain and root_authorization_ref claims.
Editorial: All examples are unified on scope-based delegation records; the informative reference to the Rego-based policy draft was removed.
